# Grasping

## When it applies
Whenever a hand takes, holds or carries something.

## How
Choose by shape. Close across the shortest side of the part you hold, near the centre of mass for long objects, not at a tapering end, tip or hole. A thin flat part is held only by its thickness: close across its broadest flat stretch, such as a wide head rather than a narrow stem, even where the head has a hole. To take a part out of a slot or holder, come from the direction it slides out, close across its thinnest side, and lift along the slot; a hand from the side or leaning tends to miss a thin standing part. On a straight-sided object bring the pads parallel to two faces, or closing will turn or push it. A thin wall can be pinched with one finger on each side of it, but only for something light moved a short way: what you will carry and turn, hold across its body, leaving any handle free. A thin flat object lying on a surface can only be pinched if its edge is exposed: push it to an edge or against something, or lift one side first. Tall objects are often better held from the side, with the hand level and low enough to be stable, though a level hand cannot come near the arm's base at low heights. Near neighbours or walls, open less, or come from another direction; the open fingers need room on both sides.

Going deep holds better: a grasp that only just reaches the top of an object tends to slip when lifted, and a round shape slips out when held above its widest line. Held by its edge or end, a long or wide thing hangs lower on the far side: try a leaning hand to reach nearer its centre before you grip an end, and bring the low side close to its seat before opening.

## Checks
Check the hold: the reading stays above zero while something is between the fingers, and width_m should match the thickness you expect. If it does not, you hold something else or a corner of it. A hold that passes the first lift can still fail in transit or when turned. Watch the reading after moves. Carrying is already gentle; slow=True about doubles its steps, so keep it for a load that has slipped, swings or tips. A hold on a very thin wall reads almost like an empty hand: when told the hold was lost, look first, because what still follows the hand is still held.

The reading does not always show a hold (check_hold=False): then judge it by whether the thing follows the hand, and measure again after each touch. Before carrying, measure the spot it was taken from: if it is still there, nothing is held.

## Recovery
If the fingers closed on nothing, the position was probably off sideways or the object moved: measure again and shift; going only lower rarely helps. Fingers stopping short mean they met the object or its neighbour on the way in. After two failures change something real: another arm, orientation, grasp location or approach. Never repeat the same numbers. If a held thing is the wrong way round for the next step, set it down where it stands steady and take it again, near its middle, in the pose that step needs: turning the wrist in the air rarely gets there.
